course: Fortified Corn-Soy Porridge for Malnourished Children
module_title: Scaling Up Production and Managing Workers

lessons.title: Hiring and training local women to help with production
lessons.body: When your porridge business grows beyond what you can handle alone, hire local women. They know the community, are trusted, and often need income. Start by hiring 2â3 women part-time. Pay fairly: in most African countries, a daily wage of 5,000â10,000 shillings (or equivalent) is reasonable for 6 hours of work. Look for women who are reliable, clean, and good with numbers. Ask them to bring a national ID and two references. Train them on the job for one week. Show them how to weigh ingredients, mix properly, and seal bags. Use a simple checklist: 1) Wash hands and wear clean aprons. 2) Measure corn and soy flour exactly (e.g., 70% corn, 30% soy). 3) Add micronutrient premix as instructed. 4) Mix for 10 minutes until uniform color. 5) Seal bags immediately. Let them practice while you watch, then correct mistakes gently. Pay a bonus for bags that pass quality checks. Schedule shifts: morning shift 7amâ1pm, afternoon shift 1pmâ6pm. Provide a free bag of porridge each week as a benefit. Keep records: name, days worked, amount paid. Treat them with respectâthey are your partners. When demand increases, promote the best worker to supervisor with a higher wage. This builds loyalty and reduces turnover.

lessons.title: Setting up a simple production line for efficiency
lessons.body: A production line moves ingredients through steps in order, so you donât waste time walking back and forth. Set up five stations in a straight line or U-shape: 1) Weighing station: digital scale (capacity 5â10 kg), scoops, and containers for corn flour, soy flour, sugar, and premix. 2) Mixing station: a large basin or drum, wooden paddle or hand mixer. 3) Milling station (if you grind your own): a hammer mill or grinder. 4) Packaging station: sealer, measuring cups, bags, and labels. 5) Storage station: sealed buckets or shelves. Keep ingredients on the left, finished bags on the right. Each worker stays at one station and passes the product forward. For example, Worker A weighs 7 kg corn and 3 kg soy into a bucket, passes to Worker B who mixes for 10 minutes, passes to Worker C who scoops 500g into bags and seals. This reduces movement and errors. Use a timer to keep pace: aim for 50 bags per hour with 3 workers. Label each bag with production date and batch number. Clean all stations at the end of the day with soap and water. A simple line like this can triple your output without expensive machinery.

lessons.title: Buying or renting larger equipment: grinders, mixers, sealers
lessons.body: When hand grinding and mixing slows you down, invest in equipment. A diesel-powered hammer mill (e.g., 10â20 HP) costs $800â$2,500 new, or you can rent one for $20â$50 per day from a local agro-dealer. It grinds 100â200 kg per hour. A horizontal mixer (500 kg capacity) costs $1,500â$3,000; a smaller 50 kg mixer costs $300â$600. For sealing, a continuous band sealer costs $150â$400 and seals 20â30 bags per minute. A simple impulse sealer is $30â$80 but slower. If you cannot afford to buy, rent: many towns have equipment rental shops. Or form a cooperative with other porridge makers to share costs. Before buying, calculate: if you produce 500 kg per week, a $1,000 grinder pays for itself in 3â6 months by saving labour and increasing output. Check power source: diesel is common in rural areas; electric needs stable current. Always have spare parts (belts, blades, heating elements) and a trained mechanic. Train one worker to operate and maintain each machine. Safety: wear goggles and gloves, never put hands near moving parts. Clean equipment after every use to prevent rust and contamination. Start with one machine at a timeâgrinder first, then sealer, then mixer.

lessons.title: Quality control checks at each step of production
lessons.body: Quality control means checking every step so the final porridge is safe and nutritious. Step 1: Receiving ingredients. Check corn and soy for mould, insects, or moisture. Moisture should be below 12%âbite a grain, it should crack, not squash. Reject any mouldy bags. Step 2: Weighing. Use a digital scale. Weigh corn, soy, sugar, and premix exactly. For a 10 kg batch: 7 kg corn, 2.8 kg soy, 0.2 kg premix. Record weights in a notebook. Step 3: Mixing. Mix for at least 10 minutes until colour is uniform. Take a handful from three different spotsâif colours differ, mix more. Step 4: Milling. Check grind size: flour should pass through a 1 mm sieve. Too coarse and it wonât cook well. Step 5: Packaging. Seal bags immediately. Check seal by squeezingâno leaks. Weigh 5 random bags per batch; each should be 500g Â± 10g. Step 6: Storage. Keep bags in a cool, dry place off the floor. Use within 3 months. Step 7: Final check. Once a week, cook a small sample and taste. It should smell fresh, not rancid. Keep a QC log: date, batch number, checks done, signature. If a batch fails, do not sell itârework or discard. This protects your reputation and saves lives.

lessons.title: Managing inventory of ingredients and packaging
lessons.body: Inventory management ensures you never run out of ingredients or packaging, and never overstock. Use a simple notebook or a phone app like Excel or Google Sheets. List every item: corn flour, soy flour, sugar, micronutrient premix, bags, labels, and sealer tape. For each, record: quantity in stock, reorder level, and supplier contact. Reorder level = (average daily use Ã lead time) + safety stock. For example, if you use 20 kg corn per day and it takes 3 days to deliver, reorder when stock hits 80 kg (20Ã3 + 20 safety). Count stock every Friday. Write the date and quantity. Keep ingredients in airtight containers on shelves, away from sunlight and moisture. Use FIFO: first in, first out. Put older bags in front. For packaging, buy in bulk to save moneyâe.g., 1,000 bags at once. Store in a dry cupboard. Keep a minimum of 2 weeksâ worth of all items. If you see a shortage coming (e.g., harvest season price rise), buy extra. But donât overbuy perishables like premixâcheck expiry dates. Train one worker as inventory clerk. They update the book daily. You review weekly. A simple inventory system prevents costly delays and keeps production smooth.

lessons.title: Planning for increased demand during emergencies
lessons.body: Emergenciesâfloods, droughts, disease outbreaksâcause sudden spikes in demand for fortified porridge. You must plan ahead. First, keep a buffer stock: 2â4 weeks of ingredients and packaging in a dry, secure room. Second, create an emergency production plan. Identify how you can double output: add a second shift (e.g., 6pmâ10pm), hire 2â3 temporary workers from a pre-trained list, and rent extra equipment. Third, simplify packaging: use plain bags with a sticker instead of printed labels to save time. Fourth, coordinate with local health centres, NGOs, and churches. They can give you advance notice of emergencies and help distribute. Fifth, set a fair price for emergenciesâdonât profiteer. For example, during a cholera outbreak, you might sell at cost to clinics. Sixth, stock extra fuel for diesel grinders. Seventh, practice a mock emergency: once a month, run a drill to produce 200 bags in 4 hours. Time each step. Fix bottlenecks. Eighth, keep cash reserve for emergency wages and transport. Ninth, communicate with your workers: agree they will work extra hours when needed. Pay overtime. Tenth, after the emergency, thank your team and restock. This preparation saves lives and builds your reputation as a reliable supplier.
